text: The assembly will hear an address by His
Excellency Robert Aba, Prime Minister of
the Republic of Malta.
I request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President,
excellencies,
distinguished delegates,
dear friends, the chosen theme for this
year's general assembly is restoring
trust, managing transformation. I don't
think that there could be a more
appropriate framing for our discussions
of this week. Trust
or more proper properly the lack thereof
is the greatest challenge currently
facing our world.
The erosion
of trust that has gripped our societies
runs deep. Where once people embraced
trust, now people are gripped by
suspicion. Suspicion of governments,
suspicion of institutions,
suspicion of businesses,
even
all too often
suspicion of each other. I am talking
about suspicion,
not skepticism. Skepticism,
the legitimate questioning of those who
hold power
over people's lives is the lifeblood of
a democratic society. Suspicion,
however, the assumption that others are
automatically looking out for their
interests and not those of the common
good is poison to any democratic
society.
No community can succeed if we blindly
believe that our neighbors are out to do
us down. Just as no country can succeed,
if it blindly believes that its
neighbors, even those it may long have
considered and seen as friends, are out
to get it. Which means restoring trust,
rebuilding alliances,
remaking friendships must be the central
mission for all of us here at home and
abroad. It must also be the central
mission of the remaking of this United
Nations.
To change, you have to believe.
We know we need to change how the United
Nations works, how it takes decisions
and how it delivers on the ground. But
we can only make that change, achieve
that transformation if we believe that
change is possible.
Nobody ever successfully renovated a
house without the fate that however hard
the work, however many setbacks faced
along the way, the end result would be a
real improvement on what went before. So
we need to show faith that however hard
the work, however many setbacks faced
along the way, the end result of
transforming this house, this home of
all the nations will be a real step
forward.
And as this United Nations embarks on
its ninth decade of service, the need
for a step change in how the
international community works together,
solves problems together is arguably
needed more acutely now than ever
before.
That erosion of trust is leading to the
corrosion of the international order.
Not the improvement of the international
order but the destruction of the
international order. An international
order that for all its flaws and
failures has seen more children escape
hunger, more families live in peace, and
more children grow into old age than any
era before it. To destroy the
international settlement without any
idea of what comes next would be an act
of wanting destruction that would
rightly never be forgiven or forgotten
by the tens of millions whose future it
would betray.
So
let us be bold and let us say it loud
and clear. Let us be utterly
unequivocal.
Now more than ever is a moment for more
cooperation, not less. More dialogue,
not less, more trust, not less. That is
the only way that we will manage to find
paths to progress on the all too many,
all true, all too intractable conflicts
blighting our world today.
in Malta, the smallest member state of
the European Union. We have always been
a bridge between Europe
and the Middle East. So allow me to
focus on two of those conflicts on our
doorstep. Firstly,
Ukraine. It is all too easy and all too
great a mistake for us to fall in the
trap that repelling the invasion of
Ukraine becomes another neverending
conflict. A grinding tragedy on the
corner of our continent about which we
can do nothing.
Malta will never accept that despair.
Europe must never accept that despair.
The world must never turn its head away
in despair. Malta
remains as adamant in our condemnation
of that invasion today as we were on day
one in February 2022.
and Malta is equally as adamant that a
just and lasting peace must guarantee
Ukraine's sovereignty within its
internationally recognized borders. That
will only come about
through a diplomatic process that the
Ukrainian people can have full trust in.
They will only have such trust if the
process follows a full and unconditional
ceasefire and the full participation of
Ukraine and its people in the subsequent
peace talks.
rightly.
The Ukrainian people will never have
trust in any search for a settlement
which involves their government being
frog margared to the table, one arm tied
behind its back whilst the guns still
blaze. The issue of trust is clearly
also central to the very worrying
situation in Gaza.
The people of of Israel need to have
trust that Hamas will be disarmed and
that they will play no future role in
the governance or security structures of
Gaza. But the people of Gaza need to
have trust that there is a path to a
just peace. It is impossible
to build that trust with a humanitarian
situation as acute as that being
experienced in Gaza right now.
Multa's voice remains unwaveringly with
the global calls for safe, sustained,
and unhindered humanitarian access
throughout Gaza in accordance with
international law.
We firmly believe that the Gaza peace
plan provides the best path towards
ending the conflict and advancing
credible political progress.
To achieve that progress, all parties
and I emphasize all parties must fully
respect and implement the objectives and
commitments set out in the plan.
And naturally no progress can be made if
there is any question of the forced
displacement of any of the Palestinian
population.
Indeed,
it is incumbent on each and every one of
us in the international community to
rebuild the trust needed to underpin the
conditions where genuine progress can be
made towards a negotiated
and lasting twostate
solution. That is the only solution.
Nobody however is under any illusion.
How out of reach unfortunately that
seems at the moment.
But nor is this the moment to shy away
or run away from the only goal that will
guarantee the people of Israel and
Palestine living side by side with the
peace,
prosperity
and stability that they both deserve.
Sadly,
any progress towards a long-term
solution is being endangered by the
situation in the West Bank. Settlement
expansion
running directly counter to the
resolutions of this general assembly and
designed to undermine the Palestinian
territorial integrity must stop and stop
now.
So too must the violent settler attacks
on Palestinian communities increasing at
an alarming rate be halted. They must be
halted. These are all essential
preconditions to a just and lasting
peace as is a credible and reformed
Palestinian authority that can
demonstrate to citizens of both
Palestine and Israel that it has the
transparency, the accountability,
the institutional effectiveness and
above all the democratic legitimacy to
be a truly effective ive partner for
peace.
Malta
stands ready to play its part in
building the capacity of both a renewed
democratic Palestinian authority and the
robust civil society that must underpin
it. Not just in Ukraine, Gaza and
Israel, but across the world. Be it the
conflict in Sudan, the ongoing violence
in Myamar, or the instability across the
Sahel, it is evident that diminished
trust means diminished chances of
finding solutions.
You could put it as starkly as no trust
equals no peace. Of course, no matter
the conflict, each with its own
individual and particular circumstances,
there is no easy way of building trust.
But equally, there is no easy way of
avoiding the need to build trust. We all
know from our lives, as much as from the
experiences of our own countries, just
how hard it is to rebuild trust when it
has evaporated.
Yet we also know the consequences if we
give up trying and the rewards that can
come if however slowly and however
tentatively we can start
if it is hard enough to build trust
human to human face to face. It can be
of course infinitely harder to build
trust of machines of the technology
shaping all our lives. Yet the challenge
of how we can manage to trust that
technology and the organizations behind
it is rapidly becoming the most pressing
challenge of our age. The sheer spread
and the sheer power, the sheer speed of
artificial intelligence is mindblowing.
It appears to be moving far too fast for
anybody let alone governments to manage
to keep pace.
It can seem whether from the perspective
of a leader, consumer or parent to be
overwhelming. There is no escaping that
this is the biggest change and the
biggest challenge that any of us will
experience in our lifetime. So much so
that we barely have the words to
describe how monumental a disruption it
is proving to be. The usual phrases step
change, paradigm shift just don't seem
to capture the scale.
And we should also be under no illusion
that the currently existing rules, the
traditional models of governance are in
any way or manner up to grappling with
the revolution that we are living
through. Which is why if we stand any
chance of helping to build citizens
trust in these advanced technologies, we
need to begin by being honest and
transparent
that governments just as individuals we
are still finding our way that we don't
have all the answers. What we do have,
what we must have is the will and
determination to act and the right
values to underpin those actions. And of
course, it almost goes without saying
that no state, however micro or mighty,
has any chance of getting a grip if they
try to go it alone.
We only stand a chance as humanity on
getting a grip on technology that seeks
to ape our humanity if we collectively
work together. Acknowledging that the
rules need to be set globally and they
need to be stuck to even as they develop
as the tech develops.
If we are to stand any chance of
securing public confidence that AI can
enhance and not destroy humanity, we
need a set of international rules that
reflect international law. So Malta, my
country, wholeheartedly supports the
implementation of the global digital
compact and wider UN efforts to
strengthen international digital
cooperation.
To fragment
is to fail and that applies equally to
fighting the new threats from the new
frontline in global conflict and
disruption. cyber attacks,
attacks on critical infrastructure,
disinformation,
the cutting of the underwater cables
that connect us all to each other. These
are not theoretical threats. They are
constant and existential threats. For a
small nation like Malta, a small island
in the Mediterranean
that relies on our connections to the
rest of the world, they are, yes,
existential threats. Tackling them must
be a priority, the priority for this
United Nations. We need to embrace every
emerging technology that can help us
fend off those threats and build our
digital resilience.
Today,
the guardians of our democracy, of our
freedoms, are just as likely to be found
coding at a keyboard as marching in
uniform. Both must work in lock step
together. Security will always of course
be physical, yes, but now it must also
be digital. That change
must then be reflected in the way we
work together to achieve our different
and common goals.
I know that I am preaching to true
believers, Mr. President and Mr.
Secretary General, when I say that there
must be no let up, no slowing down in
the relentless relentless drive for
reform of how this United Nations and
its agencies does its business and
delivers its services. To take our foot
off the gas would be to let down the
millions who need this United Nations to
do better, be better at tackling the
problems that blight their lives.
That is why the goal of this general
assembly, a United Nations that delivers
for all is so important and so urgent.
If we are to have any hope of renewing
the trust of the citizens we serve in
global institutions and the global
order, we have to show that those
institutions,
this institution can indeed deliver
in ways that change tangibly lives for
the better. We must never lose sight and
never lose faith in the values that
brought us together in the first place
as nations united.
Malta is
and always of course will be a
passionate advocate and promoter of and
passionately committed to
multilateralism.
At the core of all we do must be the
code and conscience of the founding
charter of this United Nations. But the
implementation of those values, the way
we turn those fine words into fine
actions must always be a process of
constant evolution. We can never stand
still if we are to keep cooperation
alive. So Malta remains thoroughly
committed to the implementation of the
pact for the future and all of its
associated actions. Reforms must yes
remain member statedriven and firmly
anchored in the intergovernmental
process
and efficiency must not come at the
expense of effectiveness on the ground.
Malta solidly backs a strong and
effective resident coordinator system as
the key anchor of UN action at a country
level. And I can't reiterate often
enough or restate strongly enough that
the only effective antidote to the
cancer of cynicism and suspicion is
effective and concerted action to tackle
the greatest threat to our people and
our planet.
And alongside spreading conflict and the
dangers of uncontrolled technology, the
greatest threat to us all and especially
island nations like Malta is man-made
climate change. I say
and I express this to all of you. Just
look at the weather extremes we have
been experiencing in Europe particularly
during these last weeks. To do nothing,
to stand by and just wash our hands of
it would be a moral and practical
betrayal of the citizens of the millions
of citizens who put their faith in us
that we won't flinch from the biggest
problems and the toughest solutions and
decisions needed to tackle them. So we
must not stand by. We must stand firm.
Stand firm against the torrent of
disinformation that fuels the deniers.
Stand firm against the vested interests
that seek to block effective action.
Stand firm against the naysayers who say
that because all don't choose to act,
nobody should. To those cynics,
I want to point out an instance that
shows how hope can triumph over
defeatism.
And I go back to 1967
when representing the then
geographically smallest member state of
the Europe of the Europe United Nations,
a member state that had been a member of
the United Nations for less than three
years. Arvitardo
spoke up in this general assembly. In a
staring speech, Malta's permanent
representative made a passionate plea to
the world's common humanity.
He may have been speaking on behalf of a
very small nation, but he had a very
ambitious vision. Partardo Parardaux
called for the world to treat the
resources of the oceans beyond their own
borders as the common heritage of
mankind. His demand for a law of the sea
was precient but to achieve it took
persistence.
In fact, it took 27 years before UNL
came into being. What motivated Malta's
action then is what motivates Malta's
demands now. Doing nothing meant leaving
the world's oceans to the mercy of the
world's biggest, strongest, and richest
nations. Taking action showed that, and
I quote, they belonged to all of
humanity, those living and those who
still had to be born. That spirit was ev
was evident when in 1988,
right at the start of the concern about
global warming, Malta proposed the
United Nations General Assembly
resolution that recognized climate
change as a global problem requiring
collective and global solutions.
Suspicion of collective action won't be
counteracted by retreat. It will only be
overcome by the strength to turn
convictions into action.
The phrase
dare to dream has become perhaps the
world's most common motivational phrase
imploring us that all we have to do is
have the courage to dream. And those
dreams will almost automatically become
reality. And yes, we should all indeed
dare to dream. To inspire ourselves to
turn hope into achievement. But to turn
initial aspirations into sustainable
attainment takes something more than
just dreams. It takes trust.
trust that by working together we
achieve more than we could ever achieve
alone. It is that belief in the power of
trust which underpins the values that
brought me into public life. It is that
belief in the power of trust even now
when it can seem a commodity in all too
short supply that convinces me that
ultimately it trust will prevail that
ultimately we as a world will find the
courage to dial down the disbelief and
crank up the confidence. If we don't if
we don't realize that mutual suspicion
can only lead to mutual destruction. If
we don't realize that closing our minds
to those who don't share our worldview
limits our chances of solving the
world's biggest problems.
If we don't realize that limiting
dialogue only to those who are
like-minded in reality can only drive us
further apart, we face a very bleak
future indeed. I refuse.
Malta refuses to believe that such a
future is any more inevitable than it is
desirable.
There is only one simple antidote
to the destructive power of suspicion.
It is one that may not as of yet have
appeared on many motivational bumper
stickers, but it is one that must be our
loadar. So I say
to my fellow leaders as much as I say to
my fellow citizens of this planet,
let us dare to trust, dare to realize
that even those who we disagree with the
most must become a part of the solution
and not a prolonger of pain. Thank you
very much.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the prime minister of the Republic
of Malta.
